case_data.title: Nationwide Deliberation on Use of AI in High Schools
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
The AI in Education Deliberative Polls, spearheaded by the Stanford Deliberative Democracy Lab, engage high school students and teachers worldwide in rigorous, informed discussions about the future of artificial intelligence in schools. This initiative utilizes the Deliberative Polling methodology, in which participants review balanced briefing materials, debate policy proposals pertaining to AI in small groups, and hear from plenary experts. By surveying participants before and after this deep deliberation, the project captures how opinions shift once individuals are thoroughly informed, offering crucial, data-driven insights to policymakers. Ultimately, this effort provides a blueprint for classroom teachers and school districts looking to responsibly integrate AI while actively honoring the voices of those directly impacted in the classroom.

These polls have been conducted across the US and internationally in Greece and Albania.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b: The sample from these Deliberative Polling exercises were not representative, but we hope that future deliberations on the use of AI in high schools can be representative.
case_data.headline-findings:
"Teaching subjects is not a school’s only job. They are supposed to teach you how to be a good person and how to have good integrity. Providing guidelines and resources on AI would be a good idea.” - High School Student

"We are not going to be able to avoid this... the sooner we provide training and educate teachers and heads of schools, the better. We need to make it clear how ethics and credibility are involved..." - High School Teacher

The most supported policy proposal amongst both students and teachers was that schools should provide guidelines and resources to teach students how to use AI responsibly. 

Students particularly don’t just fear cheating, but they fear losing the ability to think. Even more so than teachers, students agreed more to statements about AI tools misinterpreting user questions, providing incorrect responses, increasing the spread of fake news and information, and increased use leading to students losing their ability to think critically. 

Students and teachers both agreed to corrective penalties over punitive ones when students violate the school's AI policies. 

A majority of students and teachers also both believed that students should be allowed to use AI tools as a resource for school work and that AI tools should not be banned in school settings.
case_data.inclusion-efforts:
The students whose futures are being shaped by AI were the ones who built this process. This initiative was conceived and demanded by high school students who recognized that consequential decisions about their own learning environments were being made without them, right when schools began to implement (often rushed) AI policies in the beginning of 2024. In global AI governance discourse, the generation that will most profoundly inherit the long-term consequences of AI deployment is almost entirely absent from the table. This project offers a replicable template for meaningfully embedding youth as architects of governance processes.

Running parallel deliberative tracks for students and teachers on identical policy questions directly maps where these two communities converge and diverge, producing far more actionable guidance than either group could generate alone. Both groups ultimately rejected outright bans and punitive measures in favor of clear guidance and responsible use frameworks, yet meaningful differences in how each group views the other's AI use reveal tensions that any credible governance process must surface and address.

case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include:
This project directly embodies the core mission of the PAVE Case Book: inclusive, methodologically rigorous public engagement that gives shape to AI governance from the ground up.

The students whose futures are being shaped by AI were the ones who built this process. This initiative was conceived and demanded by high school students who recognized that consequential decisions about their own learning environments were being made without them, right when schools began to implement (often rushed) AI policies in the beginning of 2024. In global AI governance discourse, the generation that will most profoundly inherit the long-term consequences of AI deployment is almost entirely absent from the table. This project offers a replicable template for meaningfully embedding youth as architects of governance processes.

Methodological rigor of the deliberation elevates this public engagement. Most public consultation on AI captures only the loudest, most polarized voices. Stanford's Deliberative Polling® framework measures how opinions shift after participants receive balanced briefing materials and engage in structured, expert-informed deliberation; such methodology also allowed for increasing understanding about key AI concepts amongst participants over the course of deliberation. [Deliberative Polling® framework involves a random, representative sample is first polled on the targeted issues. After this baseline poll, members of the sample are invited to gather at a single place for a weekend in order to discuss the issues. cite: https://deliberation.stanford.edu/what-deliberative-pollingr] The use of an AI-assisted online moderation platform demonstrates that this quality of informed consensus-building is achievable at international scale without geographic barriers. The pre/post survey design gives policymakers empirical evidence of what the public actually concludes when genuinely informed. 

Running parallel deliberative tracks for students and teachers on identical policy questions directly maps where these two communities converge and diverge, producing far more actionable guidance than either group could generate alone. Both groups ultimately rejected outright bans and punitive measures in favor of clear guidance and responsible use frameworks, yet meaningful differences in how each group views the other's AI use reveal tensions that any credible governance process must surface and address.

The gap between global AI governance and the people it governs has never been wider. This ongoing series of deliberations is proof it doesn't have to be.
